solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Provider of course heard seethin': wages received, but tips mixed up

indicators.note: the tips of the three words are their first letters, and these get swapped around among the words
heard tells us to write down what the dropped-g seethin' sounds like rather than its spelling

parts.note: seething water is bubbling; with the g dropped it is bubblin'
wages are pay
pay that has been received has been drawn, as one draws a salary

explanation.surface: Someone with a strong accent is fuming that their pay arrived but the tips were muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' gives BUBLIN, the sound of 'bubblin''; with PAY and DRAWN that makes BUBLIN PAY DRAWN, and 'tips mixed up' shuffles just the three initial letters B, P, D into D, B, P.
explanation.definitionFit: This large shellfish is served as a course at dinner, so it provides one.

clue.text: Long flip working, Arsenal's first scored by Gunners great (sadly lost)

parts.note: to long for something is to be dying for it, so long gives die

indicators.note: the Gunners cut a line through the phrase for flipping, so they sit inside it

parts.note: to flip is to lose one's temper, to go mad
RA, the Royal Artillery, the army's gunners
a machine that is working is on

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the club's name

explanation.surface: A football report: Arsenal, nicknamed the Gunners, have their opening goal scored by a club legend who has sadly died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arsenal' and 'Gunners' (Arsenal's nickname) point at football, but Gunners here is the Royal Artillery. RA goes into GO MAD to give GOMARAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argentine footballer, one of the sport's all-time greats, died in November 2020, just before this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Composer approaching peak, Weller & Co shortly to receive music award

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain peak, as in Ben Nevis
Paul Weller's band was The Jam

indicators.note: one phrase receiving another means the second goes inside the first

parts.note: 'I'll be with you in ten' means shortly, in ten minutes
the Brits are the British music industry's annual awards

explanation.surface: A music-press line about Paul Weller's band, close to the top, about to pick up an award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jam was Paul Weller's 1970s and 80s band. 'shortly' stands for IN TEN, as in 'back in ten', which takes BRIT inside it: IN + BRIT + TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Britten was the twentieth-century English composer of Peter Grimes.

clue.text: Cross cracking new train-set's ruined

indicators.note: cracking something means breaking into it, so the cross goes inside
new letters made from the old ones: the fodder is rearranged

parts.note: a tau cross is shaped like the letter T

explanation.surface: A child is angry that the new train set has been broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in train-set's is read as 'is', a link. The letters of TRAINSET are rearranged and a T goes into them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in tatters is torn to shreds, wrecked beyond repair.

clue.text: Too bad if this little party screws up!

indicators.note: screwing up a sheet of paper crumples it, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A host fretting that it would be a shame if a small gathering went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal sits at the far end, away from its fodder at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: A modest celebration is, in British idiom, something of a party: a small do.

clue.text: Affluent youth finished something easy? Do my cryptic to seal it!

indicators.note: the scrambled words wrap round the rest like an envelope sealing its contents
cryptic means puzzling and disguised, so the two words are rearranged

parts.note: time is up when it is finished
easy as pie: a pie stands for something easy

explanation.surface: A setter teases young high-flyers: having finished something easy, try my cryptic puzzle to clinch it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cryptic' looks like it describes the puzzle; it is the anagram signal on 'Do my', whose rearrangement wraps round the rest. 'Easy as pie' supplies the pie.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuppiedom is the world of young upwardly mobile professionals, the rich young as a class.

clue.text: They may be run around inferior bells

definitions.text: They may be run around inferior
definitions.meaning: to run circles around a weaker opponent is to beat them easily
telephone calls, as in 'give me a bell'

explanation.surface: Inferior church bells might be outrun by better ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom of easily outclassing a weaker rival uses these circles, and a phone call is both a bell and a buzz.

clue.text: Unconscious insights gleaned from this Cruciverbalist Club?

definitions.text: Unconscious insights gleaned from this Cruciverbalist Club?

parts.words: Unconscious insights gleaned from this Cruciverbalist Club?
parts.note: the psychology test that probes the unconscious by asking for the first term that comes to mind, read as a society of crossword lovers

explanation.surface: A psychologist analyses members of a crossword club.
explanation.definitionFit: The psychoanalytic technique reveals unconscious thought, and literally it is a society devoted to vocabulary, as a crossword club is.

clue.text: Dadaist back cycling

indicators.note: cycling the letters means moving some from the front round to the back

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: An avant-garde artist takes up cycling again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like 'again' with 'cycling'; it is the stern of a ship. Move ST from its front to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German painter who was a leading figure of the Dada movement.

clue.text: Which side will win it? (It's touch and go)

definitions.meaning: tipping the winner of a match, then making off, read whimsically
in this cricket game, touching the ball with the bat means the batter must go for a run

explanation.surface: A pundit admits a close match could go either way.
explanation.definitionFit: In this informal cricket game, any touch of bat on ball obliges the batter to run; it also reads as tipping a winner and leaving.

clue.text: I'm snarled by trawler and soon cooked

indicators.note: cooked as in cooked books: the letters are fiddled into a new order

explanation.surface: A shellfish laments being caught in a trawler's net and heading for the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the creature's own voice, but the definition proper is the opening 'I'm snarled', a creature caught in nets.
explanation.definitionFit: This shellfish, also called langoustine or scampi, is caught by trawlers that entangle it in nets.

clue.text: See 4
"Moving" style of Vasarely's old role

parts.note: an actor's role is their part

explanation.surface: An art critic recalls the old role a painter used to play.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Vasarely was the Hungarian-French pioneer of the movement; its works seem to shimmer and move, hence the quotation marks.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1960s abstract movement used optical illusions so its patterns appear to move.

clue.text: It's only just succeeded in light entertainment

indicators.note: in puts the abbreviation for succeeded among the other letters

parts.note: fair hair is light in colour
a fair is a travelling show with rides and stalls
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in family trees

explanation.surface: A comedian has only just made it in light entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only just' looks like 'barely', but it means 'only right'. S goes between the two FAIRs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when insisting something is right and proper: it is only fair.

clue.text: A country in which you'll see black diamonds before lock-keeper?

indicators.note: things seen inside a country are placed within it

parts.note: a country is a land

indicators.note: before puts the gems ahead of the colour in the inserted run

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A riddle about a land with black diamonds, perhaps coal, near a canal lock-keeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lock-keeper' suggests canals, but locks here are locks of hair. 'black diamonds' looks like coal; diamonds are slang 'ice', and 'before' keeps them ahead of black.
explanation.definitionFit: This hair accessory, named after Tenniel's drawings of Carroll's heroine, holds back locks of hair.

clue.text: Legume men left off menu baked in foremost of Asian stews

indicators.note: foremost of picks out just the opening letter
stewing mixes things together, so the letters are jumbled
the men are left off, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cookery note: a pulse missing from the menu has been baked into Asian stews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baked' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder with 'in'; 'stews' does the stirring, after 'men left off menu' leaves a single U.
explanation.definitionFit: This small red bean, much used in East Asian cookery, is a pulse and so a legume.

clue.text: What players may perform in Rome and jockeys Ascot

definitions.text: What players may perform in Rome

indicators.note: to jockey is to manoeuvre, so the letters shift about

explanation.surface: Contrasts actors on stage in Rome with jockeys riding at Ascot, the English racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jockeys' looks like riders at Ascot, a famous English racecourse; it is a verb, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's opera is set in Rome, so singers and orchestra may stage it there.

clue.text: Litmus exam?

definitions.meaning: strips of litmus are used to detect acidity in chemistry
the written paper set in an examination

explanation.surface: A chemistry student wonders about the litmus test in an exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Litmus is a chemical indicator strip, and a school examination is a written trial sheet.

clue.text: This paper's deserted the most excellent French clerics!

indicators.note: the paper's letters have left, so they are removed

parts.note: fab means excellent, so most excellent is, jokily, fabbest
the Financial Times, in which the puzzle appeared, is the FT; 's stands for has

explanation.surface: Indignant: the newspaper has abandoned the finest French priests!
explanation.walkthrough: F and T are taken from different places: the first letter and the last but one of FABBEST.
explanation.definitionFit: In France an abbé is a priest or cleric, and these are more than one.

clue.text: Distracted alumnus I see slipping through grating

indicators.note: distracted means scattered in mind, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letter C is pronounced like the word see

explanation.surface: A former student's mind wanders, slipping through a drain grating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grating' looks like a drain cover; it is an adjective, harsh on the ear. I and C slip into the ALUMNUS letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A grating noise is harsh and tuneless, lacking any musical quality.

clue.text: One may be battered after being kicked in groin

parts.note: on can mean after, as in 'from then on'

indicators.note: kicked about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A victim of violence, battered after a kick in the groin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'battered' suggests assault; it means coated in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice of this vegetable is dipped in batter and deep-fried as a snack.

clue.text: Io has a name for shooting up marks

indicators.note: in a down entry, shooting up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: Io is the setter, so 'Io has' is I've

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of having a reputation for shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: Io is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Io has' is I'VE. IVE + A + N is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Naevi are birthmarks or moles on the skin, a medical plural.

clue.text: Fish sauce Georgia's made with spirit

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: A recipe from Georgia: a fish sauce made with a spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: This fermented fish condiment was a staple seasoning in ancient Roman cooking.

clue.text: A failing put this into action!

definitions.text: A failing put this into action!

parts.words: A failing put this into action!
parts.note: if the first scheme, A, fails, the fallback alternative comes into play

explanation.surface: An exhortation: when a person fails, put something into action.
explanation.definitionFit: The fallback scheme is the next one used when the first one does not work.

clue.text: Like missing the first festivity

indicators.note: the opening letter is missing from the word

parts.note: a gala is a festive occasion

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys parties but missed the opening festival.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means in the manner of, as in cooking terms, so it equals like.

clue.text: A sailor attending to cut astern

indicators.note: one word cutting into another goes inside it

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
someone attending is there, present

explanation.surface: A sailor sees to a cut at the back of the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attending to' reads as caring for, but 'to cut' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern means towards the back of a ship, so behind.

clue.text: Indicate more beer's needed, it seems?

indicators.note: the question mark and 'it seems' ask us to picture the glass, with its emptiness shown inside it

parts.note: another pint is the usual unit of more beer at a British bar
what is needed is missing, so the glass holds nothing, the round zero

explanation.surface: A drinker gestures to the bar that another round is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: O, nothing, goes inside PINT: an empty glass, which is why more beer seems needed. The zero is implied by the picture rather than named; as the blog notes, the pint must be the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: To show something by extending a finger towards it is to indicate it, as one does to an empty glass.

clue.text: Weather-beaten centenarian associated with endless Rime?

definitions.text: Weather-beaten centenarian associated with endless Rime?

indicators.note: beaten about, as by the weather, so the letters are mixed up
endless means losing the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A storm-worn hundred-year-old is linked with an unfinished poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is Coleridge's poem; 'endless' takes E from RIME, leaving RIM, which joins CENTENARIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's old seafarer in the Rime is an aged, weathered sailor.
